display_title: The idea of learning class-invariant features is not novel with weak experimental results

content.title: The idea of learning class-invariant features is not novel with weak experimental results
content.review:
##### Summary of the paper

The paper proposes a dual adversarial training method for unsupervised domain adaptation. The key idea is to learn domain-invariant features while learning domain-invariant features. Thus, authors design two adversarial processes: one is the ordinary domain-adversarial training following DANN, the other is domain-adversarial training on the class features. Combining two processes with two tradeoff hyperparameters along with the training loss in cross-entropy, the dual adversarial training can be done. The experiments on Office-31, VisDA-17, Digits, Office-Home, and ImageCLEF-DA have shown its performance against several recent methods.

##### Pros

1. The structure and writing are good, making the paper easy to understand.
2. The method is not so complicated and easy to implement.

##### Cons

1. The main issue with this paper is the limited novelty. The idea of learning class-invariant features with GAN is not new and has been explored by several existing methods with similar proposals but maybe different names such as disentanglement. Authors can see the refs in the end for more references. To me, this paper can only be seen as an extension to DANN.
2. Motivation is not clear: what is exactly class-invariant features vs. domain-invariant features? Are they just the discriminative features that are helpful for classification? More explanations are needed. 
3. In para. 2, page 2, the expression "domain alignment will inevitably distort the original feature distributions and enlarge the value of adaptability" lacks sufficient evidences or references. Why domain alignment will "distort" the original feature distributions and why the specific word "distort"? Do you have any figures or graphs to explain this? Moreover, the sentence "class-invariant features are supposed to contain domain-specific information" also lacks support. Why a class-invariant feature is domain-specific? It seems that there coule be a feature can be both class- and domain-specific.
4. The main contribution, i.e., Eq (4), is not novel. It is a simple replacement of binary domain classifier with a multinomial one. And what is $\ell$ for evaluating the difference between domain classifier and $y^s$?
5. Eq (5) is similar to disentanglement. What is the input dimension to the classifier $C$? The inputs to Eq (2) and (5) are different. Therefore, it is problematic. 
6. Section 3.5 is not even necessary since it cannot explain the theoretical motivation behind this paper, but only behind DANN.
7. The results are too weak. On Office-31, it only achieves 0.2% improvements; On ImageCLEF-DA, 0.3%; On VisDA, 0.7%; On Office-Home, it can only beat JAN. Not to mention that the latest comparison method is CDAN which is in 2018. There are already a lot of published methods in 2019 and 2020. Therefore, the experimental results are too weak.
8. Since it involves two adversarial training processes, the training time and convergence need to be analyzed. It will indeed take more time by its nature.

References:

[1] Pei Z, Cao Z, Long M, et al. Multi-adversarial domain adaptation[J]. arXiv preprint arXiv:1809.02176, 2018.

[2] Du Y, Tan Z, Chen Q, et al. Dual Adversarial Domain Adaptation[J]. arXiv preprint arXiv:2001.00153, 2020.

[3] Yu C, Wang J, Chen Y, et al. Transfer learning with dynamic adversarial adaptation network[C]//2019 IEEE International Conference on Data Mining (ICDM). IEEE, 2019: 778-786.

[4] Zhang Y, Liu T, Long M, et al. Bridging theory and algorithm for domain adaptation[J]. arXiv preprint arXiv:1904.05801, 2019.

[5] Gonzalez-Garcia A, Van De Weijer J, Bengio Y. Image-to-image translation for cross-domain disentanglement[C]//Advances in neural information processing systems. 2018: 1287-1298.

[6] Cao J, Katzir O, Jiang P, et al. Dida: Disentangled synthesis for domain adaptation[J]. arXiv preprint arXiv:1805.08019, 2018.

[7] Cai R, Li Z, Wei P, et al. Learning disentangled semantic representation for domain adaptation[C]//IJCAI: proceedings of the conference. NIH Public Access, 2019, 2019: 2060.

content.title: Response to AnonReviewer3
content.comment:
Thank you for your time reading our work and providing constructive comments. We provide our responses and hopefully they could resolve your comments.

-The main issue with this paper is the limited novelty. The idea of learning class-invariant features with GAN is not new and has been explored by several existing methods with similar proposals but maybe different names such as disentanglement. Authors can see the refs in the end for more references. To me, this paper can only be seen as an extension to DANN.

A: The main contribution of our paper is that we use adversarial training on the source domain data to extract class-invariant features and apply these source class-invariant features to boost the classification accuracy on the target domain for unsupervised domain adaptation (UDA). In DAT, we construct two separate latent spaces, one is to capture class-invariant features from the source domain, and the other one is to learn domain-invariant features from both the source and target domains. Our proposed method demonstrates that the source domain-related information can benefit the system performance on the target domain. Compared with most UDA models that focus on reducing domain divergence, our method concentrates on improving the system adaptability. We admit that our proposed DAT can be regarded as an extension to DANN. However, the ideas of extracting class-invariant features via adversarial training and using the source class-invariant features to boost the classification accuracy on the target domain are rather novel.

In [1], the multi-adversarial domain adaptation method captures multimode structures to enable fine-grained alignment of different data distributions based on multiple domain discriminators. In the method proposed by [2], there exist two discriminators. Each discriminator distinguishes the domain and the class of the training data to perform both domain-level and class-level alignments simultaneously, while the feature extractor learns domain-invariant representations to confuse the discriminator. For [3], The dynamic adversarial adaptation network can learn domain-invariant features through end-to-end adversarial training. The key component is the dynamic adversarial factor, which is capable of easily, dynamically, and quantitatively evaluating the relative importance of the marginal and conditional distributions. [4] proposes the marginal disparity discrepancy which is a novel divergence measurement with rigorous generalization bounds, tailored to the distribution comparison with the asymmetric margin loss, and to the minimax optimization for adversarial training. It can bridge the gap between theory and algorithm for UDA. [5] separates the internal representation into three parts. The shared part contains information for both domains. The exclusive parts contain only factors of variations that are particular to each domain. The method achieves this through bi-directional image translation based on Generative adversarial networks and cross-domain autoencoders. The method can output diverse samples covering multiple modes of the distributions of both domains, perform domain-specific image transfer and interpolation, and cross-domain retrieval without the need for labeled data, only paired images. The DiDA method can synthesis more target domain data with supervision by learning to separately extract both the common and the domain-specific features, thereby boost the domain adaptation performance [6]. In [7], the disentangled semantic representation method assumes that the data generation process is controlled by two independent sets of variables, i.e. the semantic latent variables and the domain latent variables. Under the above assumption, the DSR employs a variational auto-encoder to reconstruct the semantic latent variables and domain latent variables behind the data. Then it devises a dual adversarial network to disentangle these two sets of reconstructed latent variables. The disentangled semantic latent variables are finally adapted across the domains. The referred papers [1][2][3][4] don’t use class-invariant features or similar techniques. The methods in [1][2][3] use dual adversarial learning. However, they apply adversarial learning to align marginal and conditional distributions [1][3] or make domain-level and class-level alignments [2]. While DAT uses dual adversarial learning to learn class-invariant features and domain-invariant features. The way we use dual adversarial learning is totally different from others. In [5][6][7], the proposed methods use domain-specific features for different purposes, such as data generation [5][6] and knowledge transfer [7]. However, they extract domain-specific features via image reconstruction (which is more complicated than adversarial learning), not adversarial learning. In addition, no referred methods use source domain-related information to improve the system performance on the target domain.

content.title: Response to AnonReviewer3
content.comment:
Moreover, by googling “class/category invariant” and “domain adaptation”, we can get three related papers [8][9][10]. [8] presents an efficient multi-class heterogeneous domain adaptation method, where data from the source and target domains are represented by heterogeneous features of different dimensions. Specifically, this method reconstructs a sparse feature transformation matrix to map the weight vector of classifiers learned from the source domain to the target domain. [9] extends metric learning methods for domain adaptation, allowing for learning metrics independent of the domain shift and the final classifier used. Then it extends the method to asymmetric, category independent transformations. These two works were published before the proposal of generative adversarial networks [11] and domain adversarial neural network [12]. The MiniMax Entropy Networks (MMEN) [10] focuses on learning the categorical information from unlabeled target samples with the help of labeled source samples. Specifically, it sets an unfair multi-class classifier named category discriminator, which classifies source samples accurately but be confused about the categories of target samples. The generator learns a common subspace that aligns the unlabeled samples based on the target pseudo-labels. In the MMEN, it constructs one latent space to learn class-invariant features from both the source and target domains, while DAT constructs two latent spaces to learn class-invariant features and domain-invariant features, respectively. In DAT, we only use source class-invariant features, the way we use class-invariant features is totally different from [10]. Therefore, we think that the reviewer’s claim “The idea of learning class-invariant features with GAN is not new and has been explored by several existing methods with similar proposals but maybe different names such as disentanglement.” is not accurate.

-Motivation is not clear: what is exactly class-invariant features vs. domain-invariant features? Are they just the discriminative features that are helpful for classification? More explanations are needed.

A: The motivation is clearly stated in Section 3.2, An image can be decomposed into two parts: the domain-invariant one, which represents discriminative information, and the domain-related one. These two types of information are supposed to represent each individual characteristic of an image. Generally, the domain-invariant features are used for classification [12]. In order to generate domain-invariant features, we need to align the source and target distributions. In the process of domain alignment, the original feature distributions are distorted, the domain-related information is removed [13]. The process of extracting class-invariant features by adversarial learning can be regarded as conducting category alignment. Hence the extracted class-invariant features are supposed to contain domain-related information. It’s possible that the class-invariant features may contain discriminative information since we can’t remove all noises. In DAT, we use the domain-invariant feature extracted from a target domain data to replace the domain-invariant feature of a source domain data, concatenate these two vectors, and feed the combined vectors to the classifier trained on the source domain. The ideal scenario is that if the extracted features get no noise, it is supposed to make an accurate prediction. 

-In para. 2, page 2, the expression ....

A: We feel sorry for the missing reference [13] after this sentence. In [13], the authors empirically demonstrate that the domain alignment will distort the original feature distributions by removing domain-related information, they provide many graphs and evidence to support this point. In DANN [12], the authors demonstrate that the domain-invariant features contain discriminative information and the process of extracting domain-invariant features can be regarded as the process of eliminating domain-specific features such that the process of extracting class-invariant features can be regarded as the process of eliminating discriminative information. The process of extract class-invariant features by adversarial learning can be seen as conducting category alignment. If we remove discriminative information from an image, the remaining part can be treated as the domain-related one. Thus, the class-invariant features are supposed to be domain-related. It’s possible that the class-invariant features may contain discriminative information since we can’t remove all noises.

content.title: Response to AnonReviewer3
content.comment:
-The main contribution, i.e., Eq (4), is not novel. It is a simple replacement of binary domain classifier with a multinomial one. And what is $\ell$  for evaluating the difference between domain classifier and  $y^s$?

A: The Eq(4) is used to extract class-invariant features from the source domain. We think simple is a feature for our proposed class-invariant feature extraction. However, the simple formulation doesn’t mean it is not novel. Compared with the methods which construct domain-specific features by image reconstruction [5][6][7], it is more efficient.  As mentioned in the last sentence of Section 3.1, $\ell$ denotes the cross-entropy loss.

-Eq (5) is similar to disentanglement. What is the input dimension to the classifier $C$? The inputs to Eq (2) and (5) are different. Therefore, it is problematic.

A: In fact, Eq(5) is the updated classification loss function used for DAT. In DAT, we feed the concatenation of a domain-invariant feature and a class-invariant feature as the input to the classifier $C$. The input dimension of the Classifier $C$ is the sum of the dimension of the domain-invariant feature and that of the class-invariant feature. Eq(5) is the updated version of Eq(2). Eq(2) is the classification loss function of typical DANN. Therefore, there is no problem in Eq(2) and Eq(5).

-Section 3.5 is not even necessary since it cannot explain the theoretical motivation behind this paper, but only behind DANN.

A: We can’t agree with the reviewer, In section 3.5, we demonstrate that our method focuses on optimizing adaptability to implement domain adaptation and can be regarded as an alternative to the mainstream domain adaptation approaches which focus on minimizing the domain divergence.

-The results are too weak. On Office-31, it only achieves 0.2% improvements; On ImageCLEF-DA, 0.3%; On VisDA, 0.7%; On Office-Home, it can only beat JAN. Not to mention that the latest comparison method is CDAN which is in 2018. There are already a lot of published methods in 2019 and 2020. Therefore, the experimental results are too weak.

A: The DAT can be regarded as an extension to the domain adversarial neural network (DANN), it can also be termed as DANN+DAT. The dual adversarial training mechanism can also be combined with other existing adversarial domain adaptation frameworks, such as CDAN [18]. We combine DAT with CDAN [18] (CDAN+DAT) and run the experiments on the benchmarks. Currently, the experiments on Digits and Office-31 datasets are done. The experiment results indicate that CDAN+DAT can outperform certain more recent UDA methods [14][15][16][17]. We will update the paper, add the discussion of [14][15][16][17] and the experimental results of CDAN+DAT in the revised version. 

-Since it involves two adversarial training processes, the training time and convergence need to be analyzed. It will indeed take more time by its nature.

A: we will add the analysis of the training time and convergence in the revised version.

content.title: a method aiming to disentangle class-invariant and domain-invariant features for unsupervised domain adaptation
content.review:
This paper proposes a method for unsupervised domain adaptation (UDA) that attempts to separate class-invariant features and domain-invariant features via two different network components. 

Strength:
1. paper is easy to follow

Weakness:
1. the motivation of separating features are hard to understand, domain-invariant features are possibly overlapped with class-invariant features with a large possibility. what is the motivation for including domain-invariant features into the cross-entropy classification term $L_c$? In fact, the motivation of domain separation network (DSN) sounds much more reasonable.
2. the proposed method on several benchmarks can not achieve state-of-the-art results, which is over-claimed in this paper. Besides the ignorance of recent papers on UDA, the proposed can not even beta CDAN (NeurIPS 2018) on these datasets.
3. the discussions with two recent papers [a,b] about conditional adversarial UDA are necessary
4. while evaluating the model for target data, it still requires some randomly sampled source data? then where is the stability of this operation in the experiments? it seems the final target accuracy depends on the quality of source samples.

[a]. Kurmi, Vinod Kumar, and Vinay P. Namboodiri. "Looking back at labels: A class based domain adaptation technique." 2019 International Joint Conference on Neural Networks (IJCNN). IEEE, 2019.
[b]. Cicek, Safa, and Stefano Soatto. "Unsupervised domain adaptation via regularized conditional alignment." Proceedings of the IEEE International Conference on Computer Vision. 2019.

content.title: Response to AnonReviewer1
content.comment:
We thank AnonReviewer1 for the helpful comments. We answer the comments of AnonReviewer1 in the following.

-The motivation of separating features are hard to understand, domain-invariant features are possibly overlapped with class-invariant features with a large possibility. what is the motivation for including domain-invariant features into the cross-entropy classification term ? In fact, the motivation of domain separation network (DSN) sounds much more reasonable.

A: Since the proposal of the domain adversarial neural network (DANN) [1], most adversarial domain adaptation methods are based on the assumption: an image can be decomposed into two parts: the domain-invariant one, which represents discriminative information, and the domain-related one. The DANN model constructs one latent space to capture domain-invariant features which contain discriminative information. Then the learned domain-invariant features are used to conduct classification. The domain-invariant latent space may get some noises which involve domain-related information. Some methods propose regularizers to prevent domain-related information from emerging into the shared latent space [2][3]. DANN demonstrates that the process of extracting domain-invariant features can be regarded as the process of eliminating domain-specific information such that the process of extracting class-invariant features, which represent domain-related information, can be regarded as the process of eliminating discriminative information. It is possible that the class-invariant features and domain-invariant features may be overlapped because we can’t remove all noises. Since the domain-invariant features represent discriminative information, it is natural to use domain-invariant features in classification loss. As stated in Section 3.2, in DAT, we use domain-invariant features extracted from the target domain data to replace the domain-invariant features of the source domain data, concatenate these two vectors, and feed the combined vector to the classifier trained on the source domain. The ideal scenario is that if the extracted features get no noise, it is supposed to make an accurate prediction.

-the proposed method on several benchmarks can not achieve state-of-the-art results, which is over-claimed in this paper. Besides the ignorance of recent papers on UDA, the proposed can not even beta CDAN (NeurIPS 2018) on these datasets.

A: The DAT can be regarded as an extension to the domain adversarial neural network (DANN), it can also be termed as DANN+DAT. The dual adversarial training mechanism can also be combined with other existing adversarial domain adaptation frameworks, such as CDAN [10]. We combine DAT with CDAN [10] (CDAN+DAT) and run the experiments on the benchmarks. Currently, the experiments on Digits and Office-31 datasets are done. The experiment results indicate that CDAN+DAT can outperform certain more recent UDA methods [4][5][6][7]. We will update the paper, add the discussion of [4][5][6][7] and the experimental results of CDAN+DAT in the revised version.

-the discussions with two recent papers [8][9] about conditional adversarial UDA are necessary

A: We will add the discussions of [8][9] in the related works and used them as baselines in the experiments in the revised version.

-while evaluating the model for target data, it still requires some randomly sampled source data? then where is the stability of this operation in the experiments? it seems the final target accuracy depends on the quality of source samples.

A: Yes, our DAT needs source data to provide class-invariant features in evaluation. In the unsupervised domain adaptation (UDA) setting, we can get abundant labeled data from the source domain and unlabeled data from the target domain. Here we use randomly sampled training data in evaluating doesn’t violate the UDA setting. In UDA, there is no rule to limit the usage of the source domain data in evaluation. In prior works, researchers didn’t use source domain data in evaluating the target domain data because source domain-related information is always treated as the noises which will deteriorate the performance. In fact, every UDA model should be developed by leveraging training data from the source domain and the performances all depend on the quality of the source domains. And in evaluating, we randomly draw training samples and impose no constraints on this drawing process. We don’t think it is problematic. The main novelty of DAT is to use class-invariant features extracted from the source domain to improve the system performance on the target domain. In this paper, we demonstrate that the source class-invariant features can be beneficial to the classification of the target domain.

content.title: In this work, the authors propose a dual adversarial training (DAT) framework for unsupervised domain adaptation. The DAT method introduces class-invariant features to adversarial domain adaptation. However, the similar idea has been proposed in many existing works. The experiments are insufficient and unimpressive.
content.review:
This paper proposes a dual adversarial training framework for unsupervised domain adaptation, an interesting direction with many potential applications. The paper is well written and easy to read. However, there are many major concerns of this paper that enforce me to reject this paper:

1. My main concerns about this work are the novelty issues and that the contributions are not strong enough. The class invariant adversarial learning for domain adaptation has been widely proposed. The novelty is very limited. There are many similar works, such as [*][#].The dual adversarial training framework has been mentioned and discussed clearly in prior works.

[*]S. Li, S. Song, G. Huang, Z. Ding and C. Wu, "Domain Invariant and Class Discriminative Feature Learning for Visual Domain Adaptation," in IEEE Transactions on Image Processing, vol. 27, no. 9, pp. 4260-4273, Sept. 2018, doi: 10.1109/TIP.2018.2839528.
[#]Z. Ding, N. M. Nasrabadi and Y. Fu, "Semi-supervised Deep Domain Adaptation via Coupled Neural Networks," in IEEE Transactions on Image Processing, vol. 27, no. 11, pp. 5214-5224, Nov. 2018, doi: 10.1109/TIP.2018.2851067.

2. There are man unnecessary descriptions that are widely used and well known. For example, the adversarial domain adaptation in Section3.1 and the theory understanding in Section 3.5.

3. Regrading experimental results, this paper should compare the proposed method with the existing SOTA methods, say more works in 2020. The compared baselines are far from enough. The performance improvement is not convincing.

4. The results on more representative datasets are required, such as OFFICE-31, DomainNet, etc.

5. Ablation studies are missing. Please clearly explain which part of the proposed method works better and contributes more to the results.

Overall, this paper does not meet the bar of ICLR.

content.title: Response to AnonReviewer2
content.comment:
We would like to thank you for your time reading our work and providing constructive comments. Following, we discuss how we address your comments.

-My main concerns about this work are the novelty issues and that the contributions are not strong enough. The class invariant adversarial learning for domain adaptation has been widely proposed. The novelty is very limited. There are many similar works, such as [\*][\#]. The dual adversarial training framework has been mentioned and discussed clearly in prior works.

A: The main contribution of our paper lies in that we use adversarial training on the source domain data to extract class-invariant features and apply these source class-invariant features to boost the classification accuracy on the target domain for unsupervised domain adaptation (UDA). In DAT, we construct two separate latent spaces, one is to capture class-invariant features from the source domain, and the other one is to learn domain-invariant features from both the source and target domains. We admit that there exist some works that discuss dual adversarial training. However, the way we use dual adversarial training in DAT has significant differences from other works. Most prior works use dual adversarial training on aligning marginal distributions and class-conditional distributions to learn domain-invariant features [\*][\#]. The DAT method applies dual adversarial training to learn class-invariant features and domain-invariant features, respectively. The DAT demonstrates that the source domain information can improve the system performance on the target domain. Instead of focusing on reducing domain divergence, our method concentrates on improving the system adaptability to boost the performance.

For the referred paper [\*], The domain invariant and class discriminative feature learning method aims to learn a latent feature space with important data preserved, which reduces the domain difference by jointly matching the marginal and class-conditional distributions of both domains, and simultaneously maximizes the inter-class dispersion and minimizes the intra-class scatter as much as possible. For the referred paper [\#] The semi-supervised deep domain adaptation framework jointly constructs two coupled neural networks for the source and target domains to extract features. A weighted class-wise adaptation term is designed to align the output of the two networks to guide the knowledge transfer from the source domain to the target domain. This adaptation term aims to fight off the conditional distribution mismatch between two domains by assigning a probabilistic label to each target sample. Furthermore, a multi-class classifier is simultaneously trained on the labeled source and unlabeled target samples in a semi-supervised manner. The two methods in the referred papers [\*][\#] don’t use class-invariant features or similar techniques, they focus on reducing domain divergence while the DAT focuses on improving the adaptability of the model. 

Moreover, by googling “class/category invariant” and “domain adaptation”, we can get three related papers [1][2][3]. [1] presents an efficient multi-class heterogeneous domain adaptation method, where data from the source and target domains are represented by heterogeneous features of different dimensions. Specifically, this method reconstructs a sparse feature transformation matrix to map the weight vector of classifiers learned from the source domain to the target domain. [2] extends metric learning methods for domain adaptation, allowing for learning metrics independent of the domain shift and the final classifier used. Then it extends the method to asymmetric, category independent transformations. These two works were published before the proposals of generative adversarial networks [4] and domain adversarial neural networks [5]. The MiniMax Entropy Networks (MMEN) [3] focuses on learning the categorical information from unlabeled target samples with the help of labeled source samples. Specifically, it sets an unfair multi-class classifier named category discriminator, which classifies source samples accurately but be confused about the categories of target samples. The generator learns a common subspace that aligns the unlabeled samples based on the target pseudo-labels. In the MMEN, it constructs one latent space to learn class-invariant features from both the source and target domains, while DAT constructs two latent spaces to learn class-invariant features and domain-invariant features, respectively. In DAT, we only use source class-invariant features, the way we use class-invariant features is totally different from [3]. Therefore, we think that the reviewer’s claim “The novelty is very limited. There are many similar works.” is not accurate.

content.title: Response to AnonReviewer2
content.comment:
-There are many unnecessary descriptions that are widely used and well known.

A: Even though the description of adversarial domain adaptation is widely used and well known, we think it’s not unnecessary. We need it to make the Method part complete and the description of the adversarial domain adaptation can help introduce and compensate Section 3.2. Moreover, it can help researchers who aren't familiar with the adversarial domain adaptation understand the proposed method better. For Section 3.5, it is used to demonstrate that our method focuses on optimizing adaptability and indicate that the DAT can be regarded as an alternative to the mainstream adversarial domain adaptation approaches that focus on minimizing the domain divergence.

-Regrading experimental results, this paper should compare the proposed method with the existing SOTA methods, say more works in 2020. The compared baselines are far from enough. The performance improvement is not convincing.

A: The DAT can be regarded as an extension to the domain adversarial neural network (DANN), it can also be termed as DANN+DAT. The dual adversarial training mechanism can also be combined with other existing adversarial domain adaptation frameworks, such as CDAN [10]. We combine DAT with CDAN [10] (CDAN+DAT) and run the experiments on the benchmarks. Currently, the experiments on Digits and Office-31 datasets are done. The experiment results indicate that CDAN+DAT can outperform certain more recent UDA methods [6][7][8][9]. We will update the paper, add the discussion of [6][7][8][9] and the experimental results of CDAN+DAT in the revised version.

-The results on more representative datasets are required, such as OFFICE-31, DomainNet, etc.

A: We conducted experiments on four benchmarks: OFFICE-31, Digits, ImageCLEF-DA, and VisDA-2017 and showed the results in Table.1, 2, 3.

-Ablation studies are missing. Please clearly explain which part of the proposed method works better and contributes more to the results.

A: The DAT can be regarded as an extension to the domain adversarial neural network (DANN). Specifically, if we remove the module which produces source class-invariant features, the remaining parts are identical to DANN. And if we remove the module which produces the domain-invariant features, the remaining source class-invariant features can’t be used for evaluating. Thus, we didn’t provide the ablation study. On all four benchmarks, our DAT can outperform DANN by a large margin, which demonstrates that the source class-invariant features can effectively boost the system performance on the target domain for unsupervised domain adaptation.

content.title: An adversarial training framework is proposed to add class-invariant features to enhance the discriminability of adversarial domain adaptation. The performance gain is limited and more recent STOA methods should be compared with the proposed one.
content.review:
A dual adversarial training framework that adds class-invariant features of the source domain in adversarial domain adaptation (ADA) is proposed. It can adjust the generalization error rate of the ideal joint labeling function on the source and target domains. Experiments on 4 benchmarks are conducted. 

Pros
+ The paper is easy to follow and the idea is presented quite clear.
+ How to balance transferability and discriminability in ADA is a big issue and this paper proposed a feasible method to tackle the problem.

Cons 
- The performance gain of the proposed DAT is limited as shown in Table 1 and 2. A more detailed performance analysis should be conducted. 
- The author did not compare the proposed method with the recent SOTA methods that dedicated to solving the discriminability issue of ADA, such as [1][2]

Adaptation, ICML2019

content.title: Response to AnonReviewer4
content.comment:
We would like to thank you for your time reviewing our work and providing constructive comments. Following, we present our responses to your concerns.

-The performance gain of the proposed DAT is limited as shown in Table 1 and 2. A more detailed performance analysis should be conducted.

-The author did not compare the proposed method with the recent SOTA methods that dedicated to solving the discriminability issue of ADA, such as [1][2]

A: The dual adversarial training (DAT) method extracts class-invariant features from the source domain and applies the extracted class-invariant features to boost the model performance on the target domain for unsupervised domain adaptation (UDA). In fact, the DAT can be regarded as an extension to the domain adversarial neural network (DANN), it can also be termed as DANN+DAT. The dual adversarial training mechanism can also be combined with other existing adversarial domain adaptation frameworks, such as CDAN [5]. We combine DAT with CDAN [5] (CDAN+DAT) and run the experiments on the benchmarks. Currently, the experiments on Digits and Office-31 datasets are done. The experiment results indicate that CDAN+DAT can outperform certain more recent UDA methods [1][2][3][4]. We will update the paper, add the discussion of [1][2][3][4] and the experimental results of CDAN+DAT in the revised version. Due to the page limit, the analyses of model adaptability, distribution discrepancy, and parameter sensitivity analysis are given in the Appendix.
